Six EE Projects That
Move With Precision
Steppers, servos, and brushless motors — six builds that turn electricity into
precise, controlled motion. From a closed-loop position servo to a self-
balancing robot to field-oriented control of a brushless motor. Cheap
actuators; real control-systems engineering.

❯ project 01
H-Bridge DC Motor Driver
Spin a motor either direction at any speed you choose — the front end of every robot

$15
beginner
1 weekend
## why this matters

Before a robot can balance, drive, or steer, something has to turn a control signal into
torque. An H-bridge does exactly that: four switches that push current through a DC motor in
either direction, plus PWM that sets how hard. Build one, drive a motor forward and reverse,
ramp its speed smoothly, and sense the current it draws, and you have the power stage that
sits under every motor-control project in this guide. It is the cheapest, most fundamental
motor build, and the payoff is immediate — a motor that does exactly what your code says.

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand H-bridge topology, PWM speed control, motor direction switching,
freewheeling and why inductive loads need it, and current sensing — the power-stage
foundation of motor-drive and robotics hardware.

→ the job this maps to: motor drives & robotics hardware — actuator, drone, and robotics
companies, and power-electronics teams.
## how it works

The H-bridge: Four switches arranged in an H around the motor. Close one diagonal pair and
current flows one way (forward); close the other pair and it reverses. Never close one
side’s top and bottom together — that is “shoot-through,” a dead short.

PWM sets the speed: Rather than vary the voltage, you switch the bridge on and off
thousands of times a second. The duty cycle (fraction on) sets the average voltage and thus
the speed; the motor’s inductance smooths the pulses into steady torque.

Freewheeling and flyback: A motor is inductive, so when you switch it off the current must
keep flowing somewhere. The bridge’s body diodes (or added flyback diodes) give it a path,
protecting the switches from voltage spikes — which is why an unprotected bridge dies fast.

Driving it from logic: Two pins set direction and a PWM pin sets speed (or two PWM pins for
sign-magnitude drive). A driver IC (DRV8871, TB6612, L298) packages the bridge and gate
drive so you command it with logic levels.

Sensing current: A small sense resistor (or the driver’s current output) tells you how hard
the motor is working. It is your window into torque, stalls, and faults — and the first
ingredient of closed-loop control.

## build steps
## interview questions
Wire the driver and motor

Connect the motor to the driver outputs, logic pins to your microcontroller, and a motor
supply separate from the USB rail. Add bulk capacitance across the motor supply. Confirm
the motor twitches when you toggle a pin.
Drive forward and reverse

Set the direction pins and spin the motor each way at full duty. Confirm clean reversal
and that nothing overheats; add a brief dead-time between direction changes.
Add PWM speed control

Apply PWM to the speed input and sweep the duty cycle. Watch the motor ramp from a crawl
to full speed, and find the minimum duty where it starts to turn under load.
Add current sensing

Read the sense-resistor voltage (or driver current output) on the ADC. Stall the motor
by hand briefly and watch the current spike — your torque and fault signal.
Wrap it in an API

Write setMotor(speed, direction) with limits and a soft-start ramp, and drive it from a
potentiometer or serial. You now have a clean motor power stage to build closed-loop
control on.

❯ project 02
Closed-Loop Position Servo

Tell a motor to go to exactly 90 degrees and hold it there — feedback control, built from
scratch

$30
intermediate
1 weekend
## why this matters

Open-loop, a motor just spins and you have no idea where it actually is. Add an encoder to
measure its position and a PID controller to drive the error to zero, and the motor becomes a
servo: command 90 degrees and it snaps there and holds, resisting if you push it. This is the
single most important skill in motor control and robotics — closing the loop with feedback —
and it is the foundation under every robot joint, CNC axis, and drone. Building your own PID
position controller (rather than buying a servo) is the project that turns “I can spin a
motor” into “I can control motion.”

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand encoders and quadrature decoding, feedback control, what each of the P,
I, and D terms does, tuning, and steady-state error — the core of control-systems and
robotics engineering, and the most transferable skill in the whole guide.

→ the job this maps to: control systems, robotics, and mechatronics engineering — robotics,
automation, aerospace, and motion-control companies.

4 / 19
## how it works

BUILD NOTE
Reach for a microcontroller with a fast, regular loop and a real quadrature input.
Decode the encoder cleanly first and confirm the count tracks the shaft before you close
any loop — a flaky encoder makes PID impossible to tune.
## key design decisions

The control loop: Each cycle you compute error = target − measured, turn that error into a
motor command, apply it, and repeat hundreds to thousands of times a second. The faster and
more regular the loop, the tighter the control.

Proportional, integral, derivative: P pushes proportionally to the error (the main effort).
I accumulates error to kill the steady-state offset so it actually reaches the target. D
responds to the rate of change to damp overshoot. Their sum is the motor command.

Tuning: Too much P oscillates; too little is sluggish. I removes droop but can wind up; D
smooths but amplifies noise. Tuning is finding the balance — and feeling, hands-on, what
each term does is the real lesson.

Position, velocity, torque: The same loop structure controls velocity (regulate speed) or,
with current sensing, torque. Cascading them (position → velocity → current) is exactly how
industrial servo drives are built.

Why closed-loop over a stepper’s open-loop precision? A stepper holds position without
feedback but can silently lose steps under load and wastes power holding still. A closed-
loop servo knows its true position, recovers from disturbances, and only works as hard as
needed — which is why robots and CNC increasingly use closed-loop drives.

Why does the loop rate matter so much? Control assumes the world barely changes between
updates. A slow loop reacts late, so it must use gentle gains or it oscillates; a fast,
regular loop can use higher gains for tighter, stiffer control. Jitter in the loop timing
is as harmful as a slow loop.

Why add the integral term if P almost works? Proportional control alone leaves a residual
error — the motor settles where P’s push balances friction and load, short of the target.
The integral term accumulates that leftover error until it is driven to zero, so the servo
actually reaches the commanded angle and holds it under load.

## build steps
## interview questions
Read the encoder

Wire the quadrature encoder and decode it (interrupts or a hardware quadrature
peripheral). Turn the shaft by hand and confirm the count rises and falls correctly with
direction.
Close a P loop

Compute error = target − count and drive the motor with a command proportional to it.
Raise the gain until the motor moves to the target — and watch it overshoot or buzz. You
just closed the loop.
Add D, then I

Add a derivative term to damp the overshoot, then an integral term to remove the
residual offset so it lands exactly on target. Observe each term’s effect as you add it.
Tune and test

Step the target (0 → 90°), watch the response, and tune P / I / D for a fast, clean
settle with minimal overshoot. Push the shaft and feel it resist and return.
Make it a servo API

Wrap it as moveTo(angle) with a fixed loop rate, limits, and a potentiometer or serial
target. You now have a from-scratch closed-loop servo — the heart of every later
robotics project.

❯ project 03
Self-Balancing Robot

A two-wheel robot that stands up and stays up — controlling an unstable system in real
time

$55
advanced
1–2 weekends
## why this matters

A two-wheel balancing robot is an inverted pendulum: left alone it falls, so it only stays
upright because a controller is constantly catching it. An IMU measures the tilt, a control
loop computes how to drive the wheels to stay under the centre of mass, and the robot
balances — leaning into a push and recovering. It is the most visually striking build in this
guide and a genuine lesson in controlling an unstable system, sensor fusion, and cascaded
control. If the closed-loop servo taught you to hold a position, this teaches you to
stabilise something that actively wants to fall.

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand inverted-pendulum dynamics, IMU sensor fusion (accelerometer + gyro,
complementary or Kalman filtering), cascaded PID (angle and speed loops), and real-time
control of an unstable plant — exactly the hard part of mobile-robotics and drone
control.

→ the job this maps to: robotics and control engineering — mobile-robot, drone, and balancing
/ legged-robot companies, and controls teams.

## how it works

BUILD NOTE
Don’t fight three problems at once. Use a proven two-wheel chassis, geared motors with
encoders, and an MPU6050; get a clean tilt angle first, then add the balance loop, then
the speed loop. Tune one loop at a time.

The inverted pendulum: A body balanced above its wheels is unstable — any lean grows unless
corrected. The controller drives the wheels in the direction of the fall so the pivot stays
under the centre of mass, the same way you balance a broom on your hand.

Measuring tilt: An accelerometer gives a noisy absolute tilt; a gyro gives a clean tilt
rate but drifts. Fusing them (a complementary or Kalman filter) yields a stable, fast tilt
angle — the single most important signal in the system.

The balance loop: A PID controller takes the tilt error and commands wheel torque to
correct it. Get this loop right and the robot stands; it leans into a push and drives
forward to recover, which looks like magic but is just feedback.

Cascaded control: A second, slower loop controls wheel speed and position by gently biasing
the target tilt — so the robot not only balances but holds its ground (or drives where
commanded) instead of slowly rolling away.

Why timing and tuning are everything: An unstable plant punishes slow or jittery loops
instantly. A fast, regular loop and careful tuning are the difference between standing and
thrashing — the core discipline of real-time control.

## build steps
## interview questions
Build the platform

Assemble the two-wheel chassis with motors, encoders, driver, the IMU mounted near the
wheel axis, and battery. Keep the centre of mass reasonable and the wiring tidy —
mechanics matter here.
Get a clean tilt angle

Read the IMU and fuse accel + gyro into a stable tilt estimate with a complementary (or
Kalman) filter. Tip the robot by hand and confirm the angle is fast and drift-free.
Close the balance loop

Feed tilt error into a PID that commands wheel torque. Hold the robot near upright and
tune until it briefly balances on its own, then stands. Expect a lot of tuning.
Add the speed loop

Add a slower outer loop that nudges the target tilt to control wheel speed and position,
so the robot holds station instead of drifting. Tune so it balances without rolling
away.
Make it drive

Add commands (serial / Bluetooth) that bias the loops to move forward, back, and turn
while staying balanced. Now push it and watch it catch itself.

❯ project 04
FOC Brushless Motor Drive

Drive a brushless motor smoothly and silently — the technology in drones, EVs, and robot
dogs

$45
advanced
1–2 weekends
## why this matters

Brushless (BLDC / PMSM) motors are everywhere high performance matters — drones, EVs, robot
joints, gimbals — because they are efficient, powerful, and long-lived. But they need
electronic commutation: you must energise the right coils at the right instant based on rotor
position. Field-Oriented Control (FOC) does this optimally, producing smooth, silent, full-
torque-at-any-speed motion, even holding still. Building a FOC drive — with a position
sensor, a three-phase driver, and a library like SimpleFOC — is the leap into modern motor
control and one of the most in-demand EE skills in robotics and electrified everything.

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand three-phase brushless motors, electronic commutation, the idea of FOC
(Clarke / Park transforms, controlling torque-producing current directly), rotor
position sensing, and three-phase driver hardware — core to motor-drive, drone, EV, and
robotics-actuator engineering.

→ the job this maps to: motor-drive, drone, EV, and robotics-actuator engineering — drone,
electric-vehicle, and advanced-robotics companies.

## how it works

BUILD NOTE
Don’t write FOC from scratch first. Start with SimpleFOC on a small gimbal BLDC, an
AS5600 magnetic encoder, and a three-phase driver board — get smooth open-loop motion,
then closed-loop torque and position, then study what the transforms are doing
underneath.

Why brushless needs commutation: A BLDC has no brushes to switch its coils, so the
controller must energise the three phases in the right sequence based on where the rotor
is. Get the timing wrong and it cogs, stalls, or runs hot; get it right and it is smooth
and efficient.

Knowing the rotor angle: FOC needs accurate rotor position — from a magnetic encoder
(AS5600), Hall sensors, or sensorless back-EMF estimation. Position is to a brushless drive
what the encoder was to your servo: without it, no smooth control.

Field-oriented control: FOC mathematically rotates the three-phase currents into the
rotor’s frame (the Clarke and Park transforms) so you can directly command the torque-
producing current and keep it optimally aligned with the rotor — maximum torque per amp, at
any speed.

The three-phase driver: Three half-bridges (six switches) drive the three motor phases with
PWM. A gate driver and current sensing turn your FOC commands into the actual phase
currents — the brushless equivalent of project 1’s H-bridge, scaled up.

What you get: Smooth motion down to zero speed, full torque while holding still (no
cogging), high efficiency, and quiet operation — the qualities that make brushless drives
the default for drones, EVs, gimbals, and robot joints.

## build steps
## interview questions
Wire motor, driver, sensor

Connect the BLDC to the three-phase driver, the AS5600 to read the rotor angle, and the
driver control pins to your microcontroller. Confirm the encoder reports a clean
absolute angle as you turn the shaft.
Open-loop spin

Run SimpleFOC in open-loop velocity mode to energise the phases and spin the motor
smoothly. This proves the driver and phase wiring before you trust position feedback.
Calibrate the sensor

Run the alignment routine so the controller learns the rotor’s electrical zero and
direction relative to the encoder. This is essential for FOC to apply current in the
right place.
Closed-loop torque and position

Switch to closed-loop modes — command a torque and feel the motor hold it, then command
positions and watch it move smoothly and hold with no cogging, even at standstill.
Look under the hood

With it working, dig into the Clarke / Park transforms and current loops the library
runs, and tune them. You now understand the drive behind drones, EVs, and robot joints.

❯ project 05
2-Axis Pen Plotter
Two steppers that draw anything you give them — coordinated motion and interpolation

$50
intermediate
1–2 weekends
## why this matters

A single controlled motor is one thing; making several move together to trace a precise path
is another. A 2-axis pen plotter coordinates two stepper motors so a pen follows straight
lines, curves, and shapes — the same coordinated-motion and interpolation problem at the
heart of 3D printers, CNC machines, and laser cutters. You build the motion controller: parse
a path, break it into synchronised X / Y steps with proper acceleration, and watch the
machine draw. It is a deeply satisfying, visual build that teaches trajectory planning and
multi-axis coordination, a different and essential facet of motor control.

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand stepper driving and microstepping, coordinating multiple axes, linear
interpolation (Bresenham / DDA), acceleration profiles (trapezoidal motion), and turning
a path into synchronised motor steps — core CNC, 3D-printing, and motion-control
engineering.

→ the job this maps to: motion control, CNC, and robotics engineering — 3D-printer, CNC, and
automation-equipment companies.

## how it works

plus GRBL gets you drawing fast; then study how it interpolates and ramps, or write your

Stepper basics: A stepper moves in precise increments; microstepping subdivides each step
for smoothness and resolution. Driving it open-loop gives accurate positioning without an
encoder — as long as you never exceed its torque, or it skips steps.

Coordinating two axes: To draw a straight diagonal, both motors must move together at the
right relative rates so the pen follows the line, not a staircase. Interpolation (Bresenham
or a DDA) decides which axis steps when, keeping the path straight.

Acceleration profiles: Steppers lose torque with speed and skip if jerked, so each move
ramps up and down (a trapezoidal velocity profile). Smooth acceleration is what lets the
machine move fast without losing position.

From path to motion: A drawing is a list of line and curve segments. The controller
converts each into coordinated, ramped X / Y step pulses — exactly the job a 3D printer or
CNC controller does turning G-code into motion.

The pen axis: A small servo or solenoid lifts and drops the pen between strokes, so the
machine draws only where it should — the simplest possible “tool” on a motion platform.

❯ project 06
Haptic Smart Knob
A knob you can feel — render detents, springs, and end-stops in software, with a motor

$40
advanced
1–2 weekends
## why this matters

Most knobs are passive; this one fights back. By driving a brushless motor with FOC and
reading its exact angle, you can render torque as a function of position — so the same
physical knob can feel like clicky detents, a smooth spring that returns to centre, or a hard
end-stop, all changed in software. It is the technology behind high-end car controls and the
viral “smart knob,” and it is a brilliant lesson in torque control and haptics: you are
programming a force field you can feel with your fingers. It builds directly on FOC and turns
motor control into a user interface.

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand torque (current) control of a brushless motor, reading precise position,
and rendering position-dependent forces (virtual springs, detents, walls) — the basis of
haptics and force-feedback systems. It shows you can use a motor as an output device,
not just an actuator.

→ the job this maps to: haptics, human-machine interface, and robotics engineering —
automotive HMI, consumer-device, and force-feedback / robotics teams.

Torque from current: In FOC torque mode you command the motor’s torque directly via its
current. Instead of asking the motor to reach a position, you ask it to push with a certain
force — the key that makes haptics possible.

Position-dependent force: Read the precise angle and compute the torque to apply as a
function of it. A torque that pulls toward the nearest of N evenly spaced angles feels like
detents; a torque proportional to distance from centre feels like a spring.

Detents, springs, walls: Different force-versus-angle functions give different feels —
clicky notches, a smooth centring spring, a free spin with hard end-stops, or a viscous
“thick oil” drag (torque opposing velocity). All are just math on the angle and speed.

The control loop: A fast loop reads angle (and speed), evaluates the feel function, and
commands the corresponding torque — hundreds to thousands of times a second, so the force
feels instantaneous and stable under your fingers.

A motor as an output device: This flips motor control on its head: the motor is now a
display for forces, not a mover of loads. The same idea scales to force-feedback joysticks,
steering wheels, and robot end-effectors that feel their environment.

## build steps
## interview questions
Reuse the FOC drive

Start from a working FOC setup (project 4) in torque mode with the AS5600 reading angle.
Confirm you can command a steady torque and feel the motor push.
Render a spring

Apply a torque proportional to the negative of the angle from a centre point. Let go of
the knob and feel it spring back to centre; change the gain to make it stiff or soft.
Render detents

Compute the nearest of N evenly spaced positions and apply a torque pulling toward it.
Turn the knob and feel discrete clicks; change N to change the number of detents.
Add walls and damping

Add hard end-stops (a large restoring torque past a limit) and a velocity-proportional
drag for a “thick” feel. Switch between feels in software on the same hardware.
Make it a control

Map knob position or detents to an action (volume, menu, brightness) over serial, so
your programmable haptic knob actually controls something. One knob, any feel.

❯ wrap

A motor is just electricity —
control turns it into a robot.

An H-bridge, a PID servo, a balancing robot, a FOC brushless drive, a coordinated plotter, a
haptic knob — six steps from “spin a motor” to “command motion precisely.” The actuators are
cheap (a few dollars of motor, a driver board, an encoder), and the value is entirely in the
control: the feedback, the tuning, the commutation, the trajectory. That is exactly what
robotics, motion-control, and electrified-everything teams hire for.
// the skill ladder
Build them in order and each one hands you the technique the next one needs:
open-loop drive →closed-loop PID →balancing →field-oriented control →coordinated
motion →haptics

! BEFORE YOU SPIN IT UP
Motors mean moving parts, real current, and LiPo batteries. Set the driver’s current
limit, keep fingers and cables clear of wheels and gears, fuse or current-limit your
supply, and don’t bench-test a balancing robot near your face. Power down before you
rewire.

DO THIS
Build even one. Film it — a motor snapping to a target and resisting your push, a robot
catching itself, a brushless motor holding torque in silence, a machine drawing — and
